title: Risk per trade: the 1% example

inOneLine.simple: Decide before each trade how much money you can lose on it. Keep that amount small so a run of losses cannot wipe you out.
inOneLine.balanced: [[risk-per-trade|Risk per trade]] = balance × your chosen percentage. This lesson uses 1% as a learning example only. It is not a right number for everyone, and you can change it in your risk rules.

explain.simple: Every trade can lose. So before you enter, choose the most you are willing to lose if the stop loss is hit. Many learners use a small share of the account, such as 1%, as an example rule. With a 10,000 USD account, 1% is 100 USD. The point is not the exact number. The point is that one bad trade, or ten, should not end your practice. A small fixed share also shrinks your risk in money as the account falls, which slows the damage.
explain.balanced: Risk is set as a percentage of current balance, then turned into a position size from the stop distance. The percentage in this lesson is a configurable learning example, not advice. Fixed-percentage risk means each loss is a little smaller in money than the last while you are in a [[drawdown]]. The opposite habit, raising size to win back losses, makes drawdowns deeper and faster. A [[stop-loss]] can slip, so the real loss can be larger than the plan. Set your own example limits in More → Risk rules.

assumptions: Example rule: risk 1% of the current balance per trade. This is a learning example, not a recommendation
Every stop fills exactly at its level, with no slippage or costs
steps: Trade 1: risk = 10,000 × 0.01 = 100 USD. After the loss the balance is 9,900 USD.
Trade 2: risk = 9,900 × 0.01 = 99 USD. The money at risk shrinks as the balance falls.
After 10 losses: 10,000 × 0.99^10 = 9,043.82 USD. That is a fall of about 9.56%.
Same streak at an example 10% per trade: 10,000 × 0.90^10 = 3,486.78 USD. That is a fall of about 65.13%.

assumptions: Example rule: 1% of the current balance per trade
Three losses in a row, then one more loss
steps: Sticking to the rule, trade 4 risks 9,702.99 × 0.01 = 97.03 USD. If it loses, the balance is 9,605.96 USD, down about 3.94%.
Raising risk to 4% to 'win it back' means risking 9,702.99 × 0.04 = 388.12 USD. If it loses, the balance is 9,314.87 USD, down about 6.85%.
One extra loss at the bigger size left a total fall of about 6.85% instead of 3.94%, about 1.7 times the damage. Bigger size after losses is the wrong reaction.

explainSimpler: Pick a small slice of your account to risk on each trade. If you lose, the next slice gets a bit smaller. Never make the slice bigger to get money back.
commonMistake: Treating 1% as a rule everyone must use, or forgetting to recalculate it from the current balance. Another mistake is raising size after a loss to recover faster. That turns a normal losing run into a deep drawdown.

quickCheck.prompt: Your example rule is 1% risk per trade. Your balance is 8,000 USD. How much do you risk on the next trade?

options.explanation: No: use the current balance, not the starting one.

quickCheck.prompt: You have lost 4 trades in a row. What does a sound risk plan say about the next trade's size?

options.text: Double it, since a win is more likely after a long losing run
options.explanation: No: past losses do not make a win more likely, and bigger size after losses makes the drawdown deeper and faster.

options.text: Keep the same percentage of the current balance, or lower it
options.explanation: Right: the rule stays the same. Some learners also pause and review after a set number of losses.

options.text: Remove the stop loss so the trade can come back
options.explanation: No: without a stop the possible loss has no limit.

quickCheck.prompt: Why is the 1% in this lesson called a learning example?

options.text: Because it is the one correct number for every trader, whatever the account size
options.explanation: No: no single percentage suits everyone.

options.text: It is a number to practise with, and you can change it in your risk rules
options.explanation: Right: it shows the method. The right number depends on the person and the plan.

options.text: Because the app sets it and you cannot change it
options.explanation: No: you can set your own example limits in More → Risk rules.

doItNow.instructions: Open More → Risk rules and set your own example limits: risk per trade, daily loss limit, and when to stop and review after losses. Then write one sentence on why you chose each number.

homework: Work out by hand what 5 losses in a row would do to a 10,000 USD example account at 1% and at 5% of the current balance.
